subChunks.title: Hashing, Encoding & Password Storage
subChunks.hookHtml: The Academy's vault is only as secure as the weakest lock. A single plaintext password in the database, a single unhashed secret, a single SQL injection vulnerability — and everything is compromised. Security is not an add-on; it is built in from the start.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Encoding vs Encryption vs Hashing

  • Encoding (e.g. Base64): transforms data into a different format. Reversible without a key. Not a security mechanism — anyone can decode Base64.
  • Encryption: transforms data using a key. Reversible only with the correct key. Protects data in transit or at rest when the recipient needs to read it.
  • Hashing: one-way transformation. Cannot be reversed. Used for storing passwords — you hash the input and compare hashes, never storing or comparing plaintext.

Password Storage

Never store passwords in plaintext. Never use MD5 or SHA-1 — they are fast, which makes brute-forcing them fast. Use a slow adaptive hash function: bcrypt, Argon2, or scrypt.

// Using Spring Security's BCryptPasswordEncoder
import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;

BCryptPasswordEncoder encoder = new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
String hashed = encoder.encode("my_password");
// "$2a$10$..."

boolean matches = encoder.matches("my_password", hashed);  // true
boolean wrong   = encoder.matches("wrong", hashed);         // false

BCrypt automatically salts (adds random data before hashing) — two hashes of the same password produce different strings, preventing rainbow-table attacks.

Java's MessageDigest for SHA-256

import java.security.MessageDigest;

MessageDigest md = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256");
byte[] hash = md.digest("data".getBytes());
// Convert to hex string for storage
StringBuilder hex = new StringBuilder();
for (byte b : hash) hex.append(String.format("%02x", b));

Use SHA-256 for file integrity checks, not for passwords. For passwords, always use bcrypt/Argon2.

SQL Injection

Never concatenate user input into SQL strings. Always use prepared statements:

// VULNERABLE:
String query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "'";
// Input "'; DROP TABLE users; --" drops your table

// SAFE:
PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?");
ps.setString(1, input);  // safely escaped by the driver

storyBeats.text: The Academy's security chamber holds three jars on its shelf. One labelled ENCODING — open at both ends. One labelled ENCRYPTION — locked with a key. One labelled HASHING — sealed permanently. Three different mechanisms for three different purposes.

storyBeats.speaker: Security Warden Kael
storyBeats.text: Encoding is not security. Base64 encoding a password and calling it 'protected' is like hiding a key under the doormat. Anyone who knows the encoding can reverse it instantly. Encryption is for data you need to read back. Hashing is for data you will never need to read back — like passwords.

storyBeats.speaker: Security Warden Kael
storyBeats.text: For passwords: use bcrypt. It is slow by design — making brute-force attacks expensive. It salts automatically — the same password produces a different hash each time, defeating rainbow tables. It stores the salt in the hash string, so you only need to store the hash.

storyBeats.speaker: BCrypt password storage
Security Warden Kael
storyBeats.text: SQL injection is the deadliest vulnerability for data. Never build queries by string concatenation. Use prepared statements — the JDBC driver escapes all special characters so user input can never become SQL code. This is not optional. It is the baseline.

learningObjectives: Distinguish encoding, encryption, and hashing and give a use case for each
Explain why bcrypt is preferred over SHA-256 for password storage
Identify a SQL injection vulnerability and replace it with a PreparedStatement
commonMistakes: Using MD5 or SHA-1 for passwords — they are cryptographically broken and fast to brute-force
Storing salted passwords without using the library's built-in salt — rolling your own crypto is almost always wrong
Comparing hashes with == instead of encoder.matches() — different hash instances won't be reference-equal
Forgetting to use PreparedStatement in even 'simple' queries — every SQL built from user input is vulnerable
assessmentCriteria: Can explain the difference between hashing and encryption without confusing the two
Can write BCrypt encode/matches code from memory
Can identify a SQL injection vulnerability in a code review and write the PreparedStatement fix
Can list two properties of bcrypt that make it specifically suitable for passwords (slow, auto-salted)
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between encoding, encryption, and hashing to a non-technical colleague. Then explain: why can't we just use SHA-256 to store passwords, and why is bcrypt better?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Security fundamentals in Java:

  1. Write a method String hashPassword(String password) using BCryptPasswordEncoder that returns the hashed password. Write a second method boolean verify(String rawPassword, String hash) using encoder.matches().
  2. In main: hash the password "ArcaneGuild99", print whether it matches the original, and print whether it matches "wrong".
  3. Identify and fix the SQL injection vulnerability in the comment below.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From scratch: (1) Use Java's MessageDigest to compute and print the SHA-256 hash of the string "arcane" as a lowercase hex string. (2) Write a note (as a comment) explaining why you would NOT use this for password storage and what you would use instead. (3) Write a method boolean isSafeInput(String input) that returns false if the input contains SQL metacharacters (', ", ;, --) and true otherwise. Test with inputs "Lyria" (safe) and "'; DROP TABLE--" (unsafe).

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is a one-way operation that cannot be reversed?
questions.explanationHtml: Hashing is a one-way function — the original input cannot be mathematically recovered from the hash. Encoding (Base64, URL) is always reversible. Encryption is reversible with the correct key.

questions.questionHtml: A developer stores passwords hashed with SHA-256 and compares hashes on login. What is the specific security weakness?
options: SHA-256 cannot be used with Java
SHA-256 is very fast — an attacker can hash millions of guesses per second to brute-force the passwords
SHA-256 outputs are too short for passwords
SHA-256 requires a separate key, which adds complexity
questions.correctAnswer: SHA-256 is very fast — an attacker can hash millions of guesses per second to brute-force the passwords
questions.explanationHtml: Speed is a feature for hashing files (fast integrity checks), but a liability for password hashing. An attacker with a GPU can compute billions of SHA-256 hashes per second. BCrypt is tunable to be deliberately slow (10+ rounds), making offline attacks impractical.
